justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline across the three horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 94.5 is essentially anchored to whatever the most recent observed value was, with only a small expected drift built in. The slight upward tilt to 95.2 at one week and 96.8 at one month reflects a gentle positive trend assumption — perhaps mean reversion toward a longer-run average or a modest secular drift in the underlying variable. The incremental increases are small, suggesting I did not expect any sharp directional moves but did lean slightly bullish or upward over time.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is the standard feature of forecasts under uncertainty. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 5.4 units, reflecting relatively tight near-term predictability — most of the noise at short horizons averages out or is well-constrained by current conditions. By one week, the interval has expanded to about 11.4 units, incorporating the compounding of daily volatility and the possibility of regime shifts or news events within the week. At one month, the interval spans 23.5 units, acknowledging that over four weeks, macroeconomic data releases, policy decisions, sentiment shifts, and structural changes all have meaningful probability of materially altering outcomes. The width growth is roughly consistent with a square-root-of-time volatility scaling, which is a standard assumption under random-walk-like dynamics.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals entirely. On the downside, a sudden liquidity shock, a negative surprise in key economic data, or an abrupt policy reversal could drive the value well below 85 at the monthly horizon. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected positive catalyst — such as a major policy easing, a geopolitical resolution, or a significant positive data print — could push the value well above 108.5. These tail events are not captured by the 90% interval by design, but they are plausible.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume relatively stable volatility regimes. If volatility itself were to spike — as happens during financial stress or unexpected crises — even the one-day interval could prove too narrow. Model misspecification is an additional meta-uncertainty: if the underlying process has fat tails, mean-reverting dynamics I failed to capture, or structural breaks, my intervals could be systematically miscalibrated in either direction across all horizons.
